events.text:
Step 1 of 4: Setup

Here is how this works:

```
You give:  your resume, the job posting, a few sentences in your own words
   ↓
I write a draft, from your facts only
   ↓
A second AI, from a different company, checks it without knowing who wrote it
   ↓
Automatic checks, then you approve every changed line
   ↓
Your resume, the job requirements it does not show, and likely interview questions
```

It runs by itself; you answer a few questions along the way.

**What I read from your resume** (tell me if anything is wrong):
- Public university, USA: Graduate Research Assistant, Jan 2024 to May 2025
- Public university, USA: Graduate Student Assistant, Sep 2023 to May 2025
- Large IT services company: System Engineer, Deep Learning Engineer, May 2022 to Aug 2023
- Large IT services company: Software Engineer Intern, Jan 2022 to May 2022
- Nonprofit: Analytics Software Developer, Jun 2019 to Dec 2021
- Education: MS in Computer Science (Aug 2023 to May 2025) and BTech in Information Technology (Jul 2018 to May 2022)

**The job:** Software Engineer, AI Product, in the United States. The posting names no level; since it asks for 5+ years of software engineering with 1+ in generative AI, I've assumed senior. Your resume shows less time than that, and I won't stretch it; I'll make the most of what you have done and list what it doesn't show.

**Two questions, if you have time:**
1. Pick two or three things this job asks for that you have really done (for example, building an AI model from idea to production, or using AI coding tools like Copilot or ChatGPT). For each, tell me one time you did it: what it was, what you did, what changed. Plain sentences; dictating is fine. These details are what set you apart from other applicants. If you skip this, I'll use your resume's wording as your voice.
2. Do you have links to add: LinkedIn, GitHub, a portfolio, the paper, or certificate pages? Most recruiters look for LinkedIn.

**Plan:** a quick review: I write the draft and one second AI checks it, about 6 minutes, one call to that AI. Say "council" for three AIs that each draft and check each other instead: about 15 minutes and about five times as much of your AI plans, and the third AI only has a fast model available. Role research off, final wording polished by me, and a plain-text copy while we work, with PDF or Word when it's final.

**Consent.** I've hidden your name and contact details. They come back at the end. The second AI is OpenAI's Codex, running gpt-6-astra (a council would add Google's Antigravity, running gemini-3.8-flash-high). The working files are in research/eval-2026-10-13/runs10/sde-ai-auto-quick/.tribunal/. This text, including your employers, job history and the pages your links point to, will go to OpenAI's Codex under its terms and your account settings there. Some keep their own history, and the text can still identify you. Leave out anything confidential to an employer, and check whether this employer allows AI help with applications.

Answer the questions, or say "yes" to take the defaults and go ahead.
Quick review, please. Yes to the defaults, go ahead. No links.

Step 3 of 4: Review and sign-off

The second AI read your draft blind, as this job's hiring manager would. It said it would not phone you yet for this senior role, because the resume shows no generative AI product work, and it found one line that claimed more than your resume: the summary tied your 95% precision and recall to tracking as well as detection. I fixed that.

**What I changed without asking** (wording only, no new facts):
- Cut it to one page (633 words): a short summary, the skills grouped into five lines, and fewer, plainer bullets.
- Put your university roles above the older IT services role, so the newest work comes first.
- Left out: the public-speaking club role and its award, the graph-search scraper project (your research job shows the same scraping skills), the "100% database reliability" claim, and several general bullets (the third-party libraries, the Visual Studio Code and IntelliJ workflow, the web app's UX). From the skills, I left out .Net, Vb.Net, PL/SQL, Unix, Windows, Linux, Mac OS, XML, JSON, NodeJS, Django, DBMS, Eclipse, NetBeans, EBS, DNS, Data Structures and Algorithms.

The draft is at research/eval-2026-10-13/runs10/sde-ai-auto-quick/.tribunal/resume.md.

**Questions about facts.** Are all of these true, and could you explain each in an interview? Tell me any to fix. If you don't know a number, I'll leave it out, so please don't estimate.

1. **Skills only your old resume lists.** Nothing else on the page shows these: RNN, LSTM, GRU, unsupervised learning, NLP, Prompt Engineering, MLOps, Generative AI, LLMs, NumPy, C, C++, C#, EC2, S3, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Git, Power BI. Keep all, or which should go?
2. **"MOT model":** does MOT mean multi-object tracking? If so, I'll spell it out.
3. **Annotation:** you wrote "semi/self-supervised learning". Did you use both semi-supervised and self-supervised learning?
4. **The two 50% results:** are "cut labeling time by 50%" (image clustering) and "streamlined ground truth annotation by 50%" two different results, or the same one?
5. **The extraction tool:** does "1,00,000 records" mean 100,000? And is the 66% faster extraction the same result as 3 hours down to 1 hour, or two different ones?
6. **95% precision and recall:** was that each of them at 95%, and for which model?
7. **The paper's "top 100":** was it ranked among the top 100, or is that the number accepted?
8. **"Premier project in its category"** for the exam builder: who gave that recognition? Without it, I'll drop that clause.
9. **Since May 2025:** your resume ends there. Have you worked, studied or built anything since?
10. **The nonprofit role** (Jun 2019 to Dec 2021, during your bachelor's): was it full time, part time or volunteer?
11. **Anything the job asks for that you have done but your resume leaves out:** a generative AI or LLM project, coding with tools such as GitHub Copilot or ChatGPT, or mentoring others?

**Warnings that remain** from the automatic check: "Streamlined" (a word AI tools overuse, but it is yours, so I kept it), a few lists of three tool names, and some bullets that run just past one line.

Answer what you can; anything new you don't confirm comes out.

7. I don't know, keep it as written.

Step 4 of 4: Finalise

Your answers are in. What changed:
- "MOT model" now reads "multi-object tracking (MOT) model", in the summary and in the bullet.
- "1,00,000 records" now reads "100,000 records".
- The "premier project in its category" clause is gone.
- From the skills, I dropped C and C#, which this job doesn't use; everything else stays.
- Everything you didn't know more about stays exactly as your resume had it.

It passes the automatic checks with no errors, at 624 words, one page. Your resume, with your name and contact details back in, is at research/eval-2026-10-13/runs10/sde-ai-auto-quick/.tribunal/final.md.

Want one more blind look before it's final? About a minute.

Step 4 of 4: Finalise

Done. Your resume is at research/eval-2026-10-13/runs10/sde-ai-auto-quick/.tribunal/final.md, a plain-text copy you can paste into Word or Google Docs and give heading styles. The final check found no errors; it is 627 words, which fits one page.

**What this job asks for that your resume still does not show:**
- 5+ years of software engineering (your resume shows about a year and a quarter full time, plus an internship, two graduate roles and the nonprofit role)
- 1+ years building generative AI products; generative AI appears only in your skills and certifications
- Taking an early-stage AI system from choosing the model through production and maintenance
- Prototyping that led to successful new products, and tying modeling work to business value
- Using AI coding tools such as GitHub Copilot or ChatGPT
- Mentoring, hiring, leading engineers, or planning a multi-year roadmap
- AI search and retrieval, or personalization

**Questions an interviewer is likely to ask:**
1. Which object detector reached 95% precision and recall, on what test data, and what did you change yourself? (Tests whether you know how the result was measured and what your part was.)
2. Are the two 50% gains in labeling and annotation separate results, and how was the time saved measured? (Tests whether the two claims are distinct.)
3. What did the dynamic AI model selection do, which models did you compare, and what happened after one was chosen? (Tests technical depth and how far you took a model.)
4. What made the extraction tool "universal", and were the 3-hour and 1-hour runs on the same 100,000 records? (Tests the scope of the claim and whether the comparison was fair.)
5. How were the nonprofit's 20% efficiency gain and 25% stakeholder engagement rise measured, and what tied them to your work? (Tests how you measure impact.)

Save what you told me (your resume, your own words and the facts you confirmed) on this computer, so your next job needs fewer questions? It stays in ~/.resume-tribunal/, goes nowhere else, and you can delete the folder any time. I can also delete the working files in .tribunal/ if you'd like.
No thanks.
